2. DESCRIPTION OF THE EXISTING ENVIRONMENT
2.1 LAND FEATURES AND USES
2.1.1 Land Uses
Most of the land in the proposed project area is covered by forest. The forests of the area have all been logged or burned and so are basically second growth, with isolated areas of very old timber (Cooper and Hardin, 1971). Most historical logging was general cutting for lumber and selective cutting of chestnut, hemlock, and chestnut oak for tannin. Lumbering appears to have taken place in several cycles, one near the turn of the century and another during World War II.
Presently, the timber of the area is managed by Crescent Land and Timber Company, a subsidiary of Duke Power Company. The area has been logged over the past 10 to 20 years, and slash, dirt logging roads, and evidence of heavy machinery activity are observable. The timber species that have been logged are white pine (Pinus strobus), tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera), pitch pine (P. rigida), shortleaf pine (P. echinata), Virginia pine (P. virginiana), hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), oaks (Quercus spp.), and hick-ories (Carya spp.) (Haines, 1967).
Applicant has prepared statistics on land use for the four-county area of Oconee and Pickens Counties, South Carolina, and Jackson and Transylvania Counties, North Carolina, based on data from the 1969 Census of Agriculture (Table 2-1).
The immediate project area has little potential for agriculture other than forestry products due primarily to its rugged topography. Land use in the vicinity of the project has been classified as open space (South Carolina Appalachian Regional Planning and Development Commission, 1970).
The largest industries in the surrounding 4-county area are textiles and wood products, with about 45 textile-related plants or factories and about 20 wood products businesses (Applicant's data).
